brief.outcome: Understand the workflow, try the tools and acknowledge community support.

content.title: DeckWeft
content.body: A local workbench for editable presentations.

slides.notes: Hi everyone. I built DeckWeft for the moment when your project works, but your presentation still needs a story. It turns an outline into editable slides, with the words, layouts and files staying under your control.

content.eyebrow: A working product still needs a clear explanation.
content.title: The last mile of a build
content.body: My starting hypothesis: presentation work interrupts the momentum of building.

slides.notes: When I finish building something, explaining it often feels like starting another project. I have to decide what matters, arrange the details and check that nothing disappears. DeckWeft explores a smaller, more direct workbench for that job. We still need user trials to measure its benefit.

content.eyebrow: Compare the same words in four compositions.
content.title: One outline, four arrangements

slides.notes: Here, one outline produces four genuinely different arrangements. You can compare them without copying text between templates. The score describes layout fit, rather than whether the story is true. The browser measures the text before export, and a slide that cannot fit needs attention.

content.eyebrow: One generation request, one reviewable draft.
content.title: English drafting with Dot
content.body: Choose five minutes and a speaking pace before generating.
items: Opt in to share the selected draft
Connected Dot drafts with its host model
Review, then save a new copy

slides.notes: The generation panel is where the optional AI workflow begins. I set English, five minutes and a speaking pace, then request a draft. A connected Dot uses its own host model. Astra is the requested model; the host must report what it actually uses. The panel shows the real connection and job state.

content.title: The live workbench
content.body: Use the feature tour to interact with actual scene previews.

slides.notes: Now watch the workbench. I change a headline, compare a layout, save, and export PowerPoint. The feature tour uses the actual scene previews for this slide. It also replays a short entrance, so the demonstration shows how the interface behaves instead of relying on a marketing picture.

content.eyebrow: One derived scene drives the exporters.
content.title: Content to a file
content.body: Content and storage remain separate from layout and host packaging.

slides.notes: This is the path underneath. Structured content enters a layout, the browser checks its fit, and a derived scene feeds the exporters. PowerPoint receives native text and shapes. HTML keeps an offline presentation. Project JSON keeps the editable source. We do not flatten a whole slide to disguise a fidelity problem.

content.eyebrow: The same tool rail at every window size.
content.title: A compact, consistent Studio
content.body: Conventional icons, aligned controls and keyboard labels.
items: Generate and rehearse stay within reach
Outline and inspector open as drawers
Every action has an accessible name

slides.notes: The redesigned Studio gives the tools a consistent home. Generate, rehearsal, import and history remain available in the rail, including on narrow screens. The outline and editor use drawers when space is limited. Familiar icons save space, while accessible names and tooltips keep their purpose available.

content.title: A five-minute speaking plan
content.body: Rehearsal counts the spoken notes and estimates delivery time.
items: Choose a target and speaking pace
Check total words and slide slots

slides.notes: A presentation also needs a delivery plan. The rehearsal tool counts speaker notes separately from slide text. I can choose a target and speaking pace, see the estimated reading time, run a timer and download the script. That makes a five-minute brief something I can actually practise.

content.title: The build collaboration
items: Codex with Sol High: code construction

slides.notes: This build came from several conversations working together. ChatGPT on the web helped with the early plan. Codex with Sol High contributed code construction. I coordinated multiple agents for specialist work, and used Dots alongside those conversations. The useful part was carrying decisions and artifacts between them, then checking the result.

content.eyebrow: Browser tools, design tooling and a local MCP bridge.
content.title: Tools around the conversation
content.body: Build-time collaboration and product capabilities have distinct boundaries.
items: Browser tools inspect the running Studio
stdio MCP exposes the opt-in job queue

slides.notes: Third-party tools extend that collaboration. Browser tools let the assistant inspect the running interface. Design tooling supports visual work. DeckWeft also exposes a local stdio MCP bridge for agent jobs. Those are concrete integration points; they do not mean every host or design application has passed acceptance.

content.eyebrow: Connection is a check, not a badge.
content.title: Local control and honest status
content.body: Real host generation and target-app fidelity need their own evidence.
items: Only a selected snapshot is shared
A generated result opens as a new copy

slides.notes: The local core works without a model. The bridge starts off, and sharing a selected draft is explicit. A generated result becomes a new copy after review. A successful local protocol test is useful, but real Dot generation and the final presentation application still need their own observed checks.

content.title: Thank you, MLAI
content.body: For the support that made this build day possible.
items: All MLAI staff and event volunteers

slides.notes: Thank you to MLAI for supporting DevDay Exchange Community in Melbourne, and to Callum Holt, Doctor Sam Donegan, Advita Velury and Dhruv. That thanks extends to every MLAI staff member and volunteer who helped organise, welcome, guide and support the people building here.

content.title: Thank you, OpenAI community
content.body: Community support and API access helped participants try their ideas.

slides.notes: Thank you also to the OpenAI community for supporting the participants and providing API access for experimentation. That support gives people room to test an idea, make mistakes, learn from other builders and bring something concrete back to the community.

content.eyebrow: Thanks, Tibo, for the generous resets.
content.title: A very unofficial weekend forecast
content.body: My prediction: perhaps one more reset this weekend.
items: My own plan change: GPT Pro 200 → GPT Pro 100
Personal joke and prediction, not an announcement

slides.notes: And thanks to Tibo for the frequent, generous resets. They helped me move from GPT Pro two hundred to GPT Pro one hundred. My entirely unofficial forecast is another reset this weekend. Please do not make financial plans around my forecasting career. Thanks everyone.
